Bo County is ongoing in Israel, where Israelis went to the polls Tuesday
in the country's first election since the October 7th attack in the Gaza War.
Exit polls suggest no clear winner, a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
His supporters, however, are not giving up.
NPR's Ruth Sherlock was at Netanyahu's election night party.
Even though early results show that Netanyahu doesn't have enough to form a majority
in parliament, his supporters here are not yet giving up.
They say this is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, and he has a habit of
finding ways of remaining in government.
After the 7th of October, Hamas attacks on Israel.
Few thought that he could survive politically because of the security failures
that led to that attack, but he managed to keep his coalition together.
If no block wins, a majority could take days or weeks to decide
who will be Israel's next prime minister.
State of Alaska asking a judge to immediately dismiss a Justice Department
lawsuit that would block election results if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan
narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Patola.
Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports.
The case involves a third candidate on the ballot, also named Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department says voter confusion could taint the election
and wants an investigation if the senator loses, but would have won
if votes for both Sullivans were counted for him.
Election law experts say the case is unusually weak, based entirely on a law
that governs voter registration, not ballot issues.
The state's defense wasn't a given since it tried to boot
the challenger from the ballot this summer.
Now the state says the lawsuit has no legal basis and that the ballot
clearly differentiates the two Sullivans.
One is identified as the Republican incumbent. For NPR News,
I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
The price that store owners pay for processing debit card transactions
could soon be going down.
NPR Scott Horsley reports on a long running battle that pits retailers
against debit card issuers.
Every time a customer uses a debit card to make a purchase,
the seller has to pay a fee to the bank that issued the debit card,
typically 21 cents plus a fraction of the value of the sale.
Last year, those swipe fees added up to more than $40 billion.
Now a federal appeals court has ruled the fees must come down.
The court found the Federal Reserve, which regulates the fees,
had allowed the issuing banks to recoup costs Congress never intended.
A coalition of retailers welcomed the decision,
which could result in lower costs for consumers.
Meanwhile, an even bigger fight continues over the swipe fees charged
on credit cards, which are currently unregulated
and cost merchants almost four times as much as debit fees.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Astrophysicists say they found what they believe is a previously undiscovered
dwarf planet in our solar system.
The scientists say it's among the seven largest objects identified
in the outer solar system so far.
Craig LaMolt of member station GBH reports.
Astrophysicist Matthew Holman of Harvard University in the Smithsonian
says it's one of the brightest objects discovered in the solar system in decades.
This is an object that's actually bright enough
that really capable amateurs can see it.
So it sort of demonstrates that we have not found all the treasures
in our solar system yet.
He says it hadn't previously been seen because it's hiding within one
of the brightest parts of the Milky Way galaxy.
The object is in the outer solar system past Neptune
and is believed to be between 600 to 1500 kilometers in diameter.
Additional telescope imaging is needed to confirm
that the object is indeed a dwarf planet.
For NPR News, I'm Craig LaMolt in Boston.
The Tampa Bay Rays have avoided being swept out of Major League Baseball's World Series.
The Rays rallied in the 12th inning to beat the Milwaukee Brewers
four to three in Tuesday night's game four.
The Brewers still have a three games to one lead in the best of seven game five.
Later tonight at Tropicana Field in St.
Petersburg, Florida, stocks in Asia advancing in Wednesday trading ahead
of an interest rate decision by the Federal Reserve.
Asian chairs got a boost from AI related stocks.
South Korean shares up more than six percent.
Japan's Nikkei up one percent.
The Fed expected to leave interest rates unchanged
when policymakers wrap up their meeting later today.
I'm Jael Snyder, NPR News.
